findings.explanation: Entry initializes `done` from the fourth argument, `name` from the second, and `opts` from the third (or `null`). A callable second argument becomes the callback and clears both filename and options. Otherwise, a callable third argument becomes the callback, clears only `opts`, and preserves the alternate filename. The following independent branch treats a second-position plain object as options exactly when the third argument is callable or `undefined`; it clears the alternate name and assigns that object to `opts`. Because this branch does not reset `done`, `download(path, optionsObject, callback)` retains the callback normalized from the third position, while `download(path, optionsObject)` retains the initially absent callback. Normal four-argument use retains the fourth-position callback. After deriving headers and options, the method computes `fullPath` as `resolve(path)` when there is no truthy root, otherwise as the original `path`, and calls the public camel-case method as `this.sendFile(fullPath, opts, done)`. Thus `download` starts no separate transfer. This dynamic receiver call was not represented as an incoming `sendFile` edge in the saved graph, so the handoff is established from the inspected method body rather than asserted as a graph relationship.

The attachment header is created from `basename(name || path)`: a nonempty alternate name controls only the attachment name, while an empty alternate name falls back to the basename of the original path. The source-file path remains `path` and is never replaced by `name`. A fresh headers object is always created. If caller headers exist, `Object.keys` enumerates only their own enumerable string keys; every key except one whose lowercase spelling is `content-disposition` is copied. Consequently, caller casing cannot override the generated Content-Disposition value. The method then uses `Object.create(opts)`: supplied options become the prototype rather than being copied, so other option lookups—including `root`—can be inherited. With no options, the prior `null` produces a null-prototype derived object. The fresh headers object is assigned as an own property on that derived object, shadowing any original `headers`. These steps do not mutate either the original options object or its headers object; later `sendFile` mutation of `etag` lands on the derived object. Header values themselves are merely assigned, not deep-cloned. Finally, a truthy `opts.root` preserves the original path for delegation; an absent or falsy root selects `resolve(path)`. This branch alone makes no filesystem-containment guarantee.

The public method is `res.sendFile`; the lowercase `sendfile` declared later is a private lexical helper, not another public response method. Validation is synchronous and ordered: a missing or falsy path—including an empty string—throws the required-path error first; a truthy non-string throws the type error; and a nonempty relative string throws unless `opts.root` is truthy. Thus a falsy non-string also reaches the required-path branch. Options default to a fresh `{}`. If the second argument is callable, it becomes `done` and `opts` is replaced with another fresh `{}` before the root/absolute check. Otherwise a truthy ordinary options object is used by identity. The path is URI-encoded, then `opts.etag` is unconditionally overwritten with the application's current `etag` enablement. A direct call therefore mutates the caller's options object, whereas a call from `download` mutates only its prototype-derived options object. The imported `send` is invoked with the request, encoded pathname, and those same options to create `file`; that file, the response, the same options, and a completion closure are handed to private `sendfile`. The saved graph records this direct public-`sendFile` to private-`sendfile` call edge.

A supplied normalized callback has absolute precedence: the closure immediately invokes it with the helper's error, or with `undefined` on success, before inspecting the error kind. This applies to directory, abort, write, and every other transfer error. No automatic response, `next` call, or `headersSent` check follows; the callback's caller is responsible for completing the response and routing any error. Without a callback, `EISDIR` calls `next()` without the error; `ECONNABORTED` is ignored by this closure; an error whose `syscall` is `write` is likewise ignored; every other error calls `next(err)`; and successful completion does nothing. The public setup has no exception-conversion wrapper. In particular, invalid-path validation throws before stream creation and before private `sendfile` is reached, so it is not delivered to `done`. Any other synchronous exception before the helper call similarly propagates rather than becoming a completion callback; a synchronous exception during helper setup is also uncaught rather than routed through this closure.

Private `sendfile` installs the five core file listeners in this order: `directory`, `end`, `error`, `file`, and `stream`. It then registers response completion through `onFinished`, optionally registers the file's `headers` listener, and only afterward calls `file.pipe(res)`. Each transfer owns one `done` flag. Directory, abort, original-error, and successful-end handlers check it and set it before calling the completion callback, so repeated or callback-reentrant terminal events cannot complete the transfer twice. Directory creates a new `Error` with code `EISDIR`; abort creates a new `Error` with code `ECONNABORTED`; `error` forwards the original object; and `end` calls back without an error. Finish handling uses the same guarded terminal handlers or its own guarded success path. The optional-header condition is evaluated while wiring listeners, but its handler reads `options.headers`, calls `Object.keys`, and fetches each value when the `headers` event occurs. It forwards each then-current own enumerable key/value to the response argument's `setHeader`. If completion or failure occurs without a preceding `headers` event, no custom headers are applied by this handler. Conversely, once it has set headers, later terminal failure has no rollback effect in this helper: none of the terminal handlers restores or removes headers. These handoffs establish no particular event or network timing.

`streaming` begins as `undefined`; the file's `file` handler assigns `false`, and its `stream` handler assigns `true`, so whichever transition occurred most recently is what the deferred finish check observes. At finish time, an `ECONNRESET` is converted through `onaborted` into a new `ECONNABORTED` error, while any other error is forwarded unchanged through `onerror`. Those delegated handlers contain the shared `done` guard, so an already-completed transfer receives no second callback even though these error branches precede the explicit `done` test. A non-error finish also returns immediately if already done. Otherwise it schedules `setImmediate` rather than equating finish with success. At deferred execution, the latest state of both `streaming` and `done` is examined: `undefined` or `true` with `done` still false produces the synthetic abort; `false` proceeds to successful completion. The second `done` check suppresses success if another terminal event intervened. Because all terminal handlers set `done` before invoking the callback, an intervening end, directory, error, abort, or another deferred completion prevents duplicate callbacks; intervening `file` or `stream` events instead alter the deferred outcome through the latest streaming state.
